$$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-2x{y}^{′}+2y=2{x}^{3},\,x>0.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-2x{y}^{′}+2y=0.
$$

Let $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-2x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-2\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +2] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1$ and $\lambda =2.$
Therefore, the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is proportional to ${x}^{3}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ is the constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=3\alpha {x}^{2},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=6\alpha x.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(6\alpha x)-2x(3\alpha {x}^{2})+2(\alpha {x}^{3}) & =2{x}^{3} \\ (6\alpha -6\alpha +2\alpha ){x}^{3} & =2{x}^{3} \\ 2\alpha {x}^{3} & =2{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha =1.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={x}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
